it-2005-cs-81-1.approach: Under CAV every track holds the same data as the innermost track; under CLV bit density is constant, so capacity grows in proportion to circumference (i.e. to radius).

steps.title: Track radii
steps.body: Radii 0.5, 1.0, …, 4.0 cm (8 equidistant tracks). Track $k$ has radius $0.5k$ cm, i.e. $k$ times the inner radius.

steps.title: CLV
steps.body: Capacity of track $k$ $=10k$ MB ⇒ total $=10(1+2+\dots+8)=10\times36=360$ MB.

steps.title: CAV
steps.body: Every track $=10$ MB ⇒ total $=8\times10=80$ MB.

optionAnalysis.reason: Swaps the two cases; 80 MB is the CAV total, and 2040 MB matches neither model.
2040 MB does not correspond to any proportional model.
Swaps CLV and CAV.
CLV 360 MB, CAV 80 MB — correct.

pitfalls: Swapping the meanings: CAV keeps sectors per track constant, so outer tracks waste density.
it-2005-cs-81-1.verification: Outer/inner circumference ratio = 8, so the outer CLV track holds 80 MB; the sum 10 + 20 + … + 80 = 360.

it-2005-cs-81-2.approach: Time = seek (inner → outer track) + rotational wait until sector 4 starts + transfer of the sectors holding 1 MB; the platter keeps rotating during the seek.
it-2005-cs-81-2.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Rotation | 6000 RPM ⇒ 10 ms/rev |
| Sectors/track | 20 ⇒ 0.5 ms each |
| Data/sector (CAV) | 10 MB / 20 = 0.5 MB |
| Seek distance | 4 − 0.5 = 3.5 cm |

steps.title: Seek
steps.body: $\dfrac{0.035\text{ m}}{10\text{ m/s}}=3.5$ ms.

steps.title: Where the head is after the seek
steps.body: During 3.5 ms the disk turns $3.5/0.5=7$ sectors: from the end of sector 5 to the end of sector 12.

steps.title: Rotational wait
steps.body: Sector 4 starts at the end of sector 3. From the end of sector 12: sectors 13–20 (8) and 1–3 (3) = 11 sectors $=11\times0.5=5.5$ ms.

steps.title: Transfer and total
steps.body: 1 MB = 2 sectors = 1 ms. Total $=3.5+5.5+1=10$ ms.

optionAnalysis.reason: 13.5 ms adds a further wait of 3.5 ms (seek not overlapped with rotation).
9.5 ms is one sector short (sector off-by-one).
20 ms is two full rotations, far more than needed.

pitfalls: Forgetting that the platter rotates during the seek.
Using CLV capacities: the drive here is CAV, so every sector holds 0.5 MB.
it-2005-cs-81-2.verification: Elapsed 10 ms is exactly one revolution: the head ends at the end of sector 5 again, which is the end of the second sector read (4, 5). Consistent.

it-2005-cs-82-1.approach: In (record-at-a-time) nested-loop join the inner table is scanned once per outer record: cost = b_outer + n_outer × b_inner. Try both orders.

steps.title: Choose
steps.body: The smaller cost, 32020, uses T2 (fewer records) in the outer loop.

optionAnalysis.reason: 800000 = 2000 × 400 counts record pairs, not block accesses.
40080 is the cost with T1 outside — not the most appropriate choice.
32020 — T2 outside, the minimum.
100 = 80 + 20 is a single scan of each table (only possible with enough memory).

pitfalls: Picking the table with fewer blocks without comparing record counts.
it-2005-cs-82-1.verification: Table T1: 2000 records, 80 blocks; T2: 400 records, 20 blocks; one buffer block per table. Each outer record forces a full inner scan, so 400 × 80 + 20 = 32020.

it-2005-cs-82-2.approach: Block nested-loop join scans the inner table once per outer block: cost = b_outer + b_outer × b_inner. Subtract from the 32020 found in 82.1.

steps.title: Reduction
steps.body: Nested-loop cost from 82.1 minus block nested-loop cost: $32020-1620=30400$ fewer block accesses.

optionAnalysis.reason: Block nested-loop join is much cheaper, so the reduction is not 0.
38400 = 40080 − 1680 uses T1 as outer in both algorithms.
798400 is based on the record-pair count, not block accesses.

pitfalls: Mixing outer-table choices between the two algorithms.
it-2005-cs-82-2.verification: Table T1: 2000 records, 80 blocks; T2: 400 records, 20 blocks; one buffer block per table. 32020 − 1620 = 30400 (both with T2 outside).

it-2005-cs-83-1.approach: Only the rule E → E + E can cause ambiguity, because * always comes with its own parentheses. A string is ambiguous only if it has two or more + at the same parenthesis level.

steps.title: Where the ambiguity is
steps.body: $(E*E)$ is fully bracketed, so it parses one way. $E+E$ with operands $x_1+x_2+x_3$ can group as $(x_1+x_2)+x_3$ or $x_1+(x_2+x_3)$.

steps.title: Count + at the top level
steps.body: A: three + at the top level — ambiguous. B, C: a single top-level +. D: one + inside the outer brackets and that bracket level has only one +.

optionAnalysis.reason: Three + at the same level ⇒ several groupings ⇒ several parse trees.
One + whose right operand is a fully bracketed product — unique parse.
One + whose left operand is a fully bracketed product — unique parse.
Inside the outer (E*E), the left E is id and the right E is id + id with one + — unique parse.

it-2005-cs-83-1.verification: Each of B, C, D has at most one + per parenthesis level.

it-2005-cs-83-2.approach: Parse trees of x₁+x₂+x₃+x₄ under E → E + E correspond to full binary bracketings of 4 operands, counted by the Catalan number C₃.

optionAnalysis.reason: C₃ = 5 — correct.
4 misses one bracketing (usually (a+b)+(c+d)).
3 is the number of + signs, not trees.
2 would be the count for three operands (C₂).

it-2005-cs-83-2.verification: Split by the root +: left part sizes 1,2,3 give C₀C₂ + C₁C₁ + C₂C₀ = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5.

it-2005-cs-84-1.approach: The first loop is candidate elimination: compare candidate i with each later j. If i → j is absent, j cannot be the sink, so keep i; if i → j exists, i cannot be the sink, so make j the candidate.

steps.title: E1: when to skip j
steps.body: Keep scanning while $A[i][j]=0$: $j$ lacks the edge $i\to j$, so $j$ is not a sink. Hence E1 = \`!A[i][j]\`.

steps.title: E2: when the loop stops
steps.body: It stops at the first $j$ with $A[i][j]=1$; then $i$ has an outgoing edge and cannot be the sink, so the new candidate is $j$: E2 = \`i = j\`.

steps.title: Why it ends with the only candidate
steps.body: Every vertex skipped or abandoned is eliminated, so after one pass i is the only possible sink, checked in O(n) by the second loop.

optionAnalysis.reason: With E1 = A[i][j], j is skipped exactly when i has an edge to it — the opposite of the elimination rule.
i = j + 1 skips vertex j, which may well be the sink.
Skip non-neighbours, jump to the first out-neighbour — correct.
Both the condition and the update are wrong.

pitfalls: Advancing to j + 1 and losing the only remaining candidate.
it-2005-cs-84-1.verification: For a 3-vertex graph where 2 is the sink: i=0, A[0][1]=0 so skip 1, A[0][2]=1 so i=2; j=3 ends the loop with i=2.

it-2005-cs-84-2.approach: Candidate i is a sink iff for every j ≠ i: A[i][j] = 0 and A[j][i] = 1. flag must be cleared when either condition fails.

steps.title: Sink condition
steps.body: For all $j\ne i$: $\lnot A[i][j]\land A[j][i]$.

steps.title: Negate for flag = 0
steps.body: $\lnot(\lnot A[i][j]\land A[j][i])=A[i][j]\lor\lnot A[j][i]$ ⇒ E3 = \`(A[i][j] || !A[j][i])\`.

optionAnalysis.reason: Requires both failures at once; misses a vertex that, say, has an outgoing edge and also an incoming one.
This is the condition for j being fine — it would clear flag for a true sink.
Also true for a correct sink (A[j][i] = 1), so it would reject every sink.
Clears flag exactly when the sink property fails for some j — correct.

it-2005-cs-84-2.verification: For a real sink every j gives A[i][j] = 0 and A[j][i] = 1, so E3 is false for all j and flag stays 1.

it-2005-cs-85-1.approach: After distance-vector routing stabilises, each cost equals the BFS hop distance (unit edge costs). Check each table against the true distances; one wrong entry rules a table out.
it-2005-cs-85-1.given: Edges: A–B, A–C, B–C, B–D, C–D, C–E, D–E, D–F, E–F.

steps.title: Spot-check A, C and D
steps.body:
- A to D: A–B–D is **2**, table A says 3 ✗.
- C to F: C–D–F is **2**, table C says 3 ✗.
- D to A: D–B–A is **2**, table D says 3 ✗.

steps.title: BFS from B
steps.body: Distance 1: A, C, D. Distance 2: E (via C or D), F (via D).

steps.title: Compare with table B
steps.body: A 1 (A), C 1 (C), D 1 (D), E 2 via C, F 2 via D — every entry is correct.

optionAnalysis.reason: Cost A → D is 2 (A–B–D) and A → E is 2 (A–C–E), not 3; A → F is 3, not 4.
Cost C → F is 2 (C–D–F or C–E–F), not 3.
Every entry of B's table matches the BFS distances — correct.
Cost D → A is 2 (D–B–A or D–C–A), not 3.

it-2005-cs-85-1.verification: Recomputed BFS from every node; only table B is consistent.

it-2005-cs-85-2.approach: When A fails, B and C still hear stale routes to A from each other and from D, E, F, so distance-vector suffers count-to-infinity: costs grow by about 1 per update interval and never reach ∞ in 100 intervals.

steps.title: Before failure
steps.body: Costs to A: B 1, C 1, D 2, E 2, F 3.

steps.title: First updates
steps.body:
B now sees A only through C (1) or D (2), so B = 1 + 1 = 2; likewise C = 2. D, E stay 2, F 3.
Next round: B, C, D, E all = 3; F = 3.

steps.title: Steady growth
steps.body: From round 2 on every node takes 1 + (a neighbour's cost) and all costs rise by exactly 1 per round: after round t the cost is t + 1.

steps.title: At t + 100
steps.body: After 100 update intervals F's cost is $100+1=101$: larger than 100 but still finite.

optionAnalysis.reason: Count-to-infinity gives 101 after 100 intervals — > 100 and finite.
Distance vector has no way to learn the loss quickly; ∞ is never reached in 100 rounds.
Stale cost 3 is replaced after the first few rounds.
Costs keep rising beyond 100 (they are 101 at t + 100).

pitfalls: Assuming poisoned reverse or split horizon — the described protocol uses neither.
it-2005-cs-85-2.verification: Simulated the synchronous updates: F → A cost after rounds 1..5 is 3, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 101 after round 100.
